title: Nikole Hannah-Jones’ New York school dilemma is shared by Black parents everywhere
author: Keturah Kendrick
summary: Keturah Kendrick, who taught English for ten years at a philanthropist-founded New York City school serving mostly Black and Latino students, responds to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay from inside the system. She adopts the framing of Najya's middle school principal that New York school segregation is a Venn diagram of race, class, and ability. Kendrick admits her own school's 100 percent graduation and college acceptance rates depended on rarely admitting sixth graders who scored below proficient, a form of segregation by ability that many applaud. Hannah-Jones's daughter attended an Urban Assembly school that does not screen, and Kendrick argues she might have had a different grievance at a screened school, as some of Kendrick's former students later discovered their own learning gaps in elite colleges. Her conclusion is that Black parents face false choices built on at least one tier of segregation, leaving their daughters without the education they deserve.
points: Kendrick describes a successful school whose results relied on screening out academically behind applicants.
Majority Black and brown schools are often praised for beating racial segregation by leaning on segregation by ability.
Najya's Urban Assembly school did not screen for test scores, unlike the network where Kendrick taught.
Former students from Kendrick's selective school still found learning gaps and isolation in elite colleges.
Black parents, she argues, face rigid either-or choices that each rest on some form of segregation.
quotes: Trained as an English teacher in New York City, I’m a Black woman who taught for 10 years at a school similar in all ways but one to the middle school where Hannah-Jones sent her daughter.
As her daughter’s middle school principal, Emily Paige, frames it: Segregation in New York City schools is a Venn diagram of race, class and ability.
The truth of the matter is, my school was highly successful because we rarely accepted sixth graders who hadn’t gotten at least a 3 out of 4 on their state English and math tests.

What I hate for Najya is that she would probably have a different gripe if her mother had enrolled her in one of the considerable number of diverse schools that screen for students who are easier to teach.
As a 51-year-old woman who worked within that school system, I understand what Najya doesn’t: Black parents are presented with false “choices” from the start.

However, the fact that so many Black parents are presented with such a rigid either-or decision only guarantees that Black girls who want a rigorous academic setting and a safe environment to foster their identity will never have the education they truly deserve.
